title: Psalm 137: By the Rivers of Babylon
summary: Exiles in Babylon remember how they sat by its rivers and wept for Zion, hanging up their harps when their captors demanded songs of joy. The singer swears never to forget Jerusalem, then turns to God with a cry for justice against Edom, which cheered Jerusalem's destruction, and against Babylon, ending with a blessing on whoever repays Babylon by dashing its infants against the rocks.
story: Psalm 137 is one of the few psalms whose own words name a specific time and place: Babylon, after the fall of Jerusalem. It comes directly after Psalm 136, with its twenty-six declarations that God's loving devotion endures forever, and the juxtaposition is intentional or at least striking. The people who once sang that refrain in the temple now cannot sing at all. The psalm sits in Book V of the Psalter (Psalms 107 to 150), a collection shaped for a people who had lived through exile and were learning to pray again. After it comes Psalm 138, a thanksgiving of David that begins by praising God before the gods, as though the Psalter answers the question of verse 4 (how can we sing?) by beginning to sing again.
historical:
The Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem more than once. In 597 BC he took King Jehoiachin and many leading citizens into exile, and in 587 or 586 BC his army broke through the walls, burned the temple, and deported much of the remaining population (2 Kings 24 and 25). The exiles were settled in communities in southern Mesopotamia; Ezekiel lived among them by the Kebar canal (Ezekiel 1:1). Babylon lay on the Euphrates and was laced with irrigation canals, which is why the psalm speaks of the rivers of Babylon.

The psalm has no superscription. The past tense of the opening (“we sat and wept”) leads many interpreters to think it was written after the exile ended, perhaps by someone who had returned to Jerusalem and was remembering, though others read it as composed in Babylon itself. Edom, named in verse 7, was Israel's neighbor to the southeast, descended according to Genesis from Esau, Jacob's brother. Several prophets condemn Edom for rejoicing over Jerusalem's fall and for helping the invaders (Obadiah 10-14, Lamentations 4:21-22, and Ezekiel 25:12-14). Babylon itself fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC, and in 538 BC Cyrus allowed the exiles to return.
cultural:
The harp or lyre (kinnor) was the instrument of Israel's temple music and of David himself. Hanging it on the trees was a refusal to play. The captors' demand for songs of Zion may have been mockery, or simply curiosity about a conquered people's famous hymns, but for the exiles those songs belonged to the LORD and to his house. Many of them celebrated Zion as the city God would never let fall (Psalms 46 and 48). To sing them as entertainment in the capital of the empire that had just destroyed Zion would have been unbearable.

The oath of verses 5 and 6 is a self-curse, a common form of solemn promise in the ancient Near East: may this happen to me if I break my word. A musician's right hand plays the strings and his tongue sings, so the singer stakes the very powers of his craft on remembering Jerusalem. The cry of verses 8 and 9 reflects the grim realities of ancient siege warfare, in which conquering armies routinely killed children to end a dynasty or a people's future. The prophets record such atrocities as the ordinary cruelty of war (2 Kings 8:12 and Hosea 13:16), and Isaiah's oracle against Babylon uses the same image for Babylon's own coming fall (Isaiah 13:16).
literary: Psalm 137 is a communal lament that moves through three movements, each with its own tone. Verses 1 to 4 are memory and grief, told as a scene: the rivers, the willows, the hanging harps, the taunting request. Verses 5 and 6 switch suddenly to the first person singular and to an oath, as one voice speaks for the community. Verses 7 to 9 turn to God and to Israel's enemies, first a plea that the LORD remember Edom, then a direct address to Babylon. The verb remember ties the psalm together: the exiles remember Zion (verse 1), the singer vows not to forget but to remember Jerusalem (verses 5 and 6), and the singer asks God to remember what Edom did (verse 7). The two blessed statements in verses 8 and 9 use the same word that opens the whole Psalter (Psalm 1:1), which makes their content all the more shocking.

outline.t: Weeping by the rivers: how can we sing?
An oath never to forget Jerusalem
The cry for justice against Babylon

doctrines.note: The psalm gives words to grief that has not yet been comforted. Scripture includes this prayer, raw and unresolved, and in doing so it permits the wounded to bring their whole experience, including their rage, before God.
The cry for repayment appeals to the principle that God will do to the oppressor as the oppressor has done. The psalmist does not take vengeance himself; he asks God to remember and to act.
Lament is prayer. The exiles cannot sing the songs of joy, but they can still speak to the LORD, and their honest anguish is addressed to him rather than turned away from him.

words.note: Zakar, to remember. In the Old Testament remembering is more than recalling a fact; it means acting in keeping with what is recalled. When the exiles remember Zion, they grieve and remain loyal. When they ask the LORD to remember Edom, they are asking him to act in justice, just as when God remembered Noah (Genesis 8:1) he acted to save him.

Kinnor, lyre or harp. This stringed instrument, held in the arms and plucked, was used in Israel's worship and was associated with David. Hanging the lyres on the willows is a picture of joy suspended. The instrument survives, but the song cannot be sung in that place.

Esher, blessed or happy. The word describes the flourishing of someone whose life is in line with God's order, and it opens the Psalter in Psalm 1:1. Its use in verses 8 and 9 is one of the most disturbing in Scripture: the singer calls happy the one who repays Babylon. The word shows how deeply the exiles longed for justice to be done.

Gemul, recompense or repayment. It describes what a person has done and what comes back to them in return. Verse 8 asks that Babylon receive back what it has dealt out, the logic of justice found in the law's principle of proportional repayment (Exodus 21:23-25). The cry is not for gratuitous cruelty but for the same measure Babylon had used.

christ: The link to Christ is not in a prediction but in how the New Testament handles the cry for vengeance. Jesus wept over Jerusalem and foresaw its fall (Luke 19:41-44), sharing the psalmist's grief for the city. But he taught his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matthew 5:44), and on the cross he prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34). Paul tells believers never to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath (Romans 12:19), which is what the psalmist does: he hands his rage to God rather than acting on it. Revelation takes up the fall of Babylon as the symbol of every proud, violent power (Revelation 18), and the cry of the souls under the altar, how long before you avenge our blood (Revelation 6:10), shows the church praying something like this psalm. In Christ the demand for justice is not cancelled; it is met, since God judges evil at the cross and promises to set the world right at the end.

hard.q: How can Scripture call someone blessed for smashing infants against rocks?
hard.a:
Verse 9 is one of the hardest lines in the Bible, and it should not be softened. The singer, speaking for people who had seen their own children killed and their city burned, calls blessed whoever does the same to Babylon. Several things help us read it honestly. First, the psalm is a prayer, not a command or a policy. It is addressed to God and hands the demand for justice to him; nowhere does the psalmist take up the sword himself. Second, it repeats the logic of repayment (as you have done to us), and it echoes the prophets' announcements of Babylon's fall, including Isaiah 13:16. The exiles had seen what Babylon's armies did to Jerusalem, where young and old fell in the streets and children died in the siege (Lamentations 2:20-21), and they were asking for justice in the same terms. Third, Scripture includes this prayer because it tells the truth about what suffering does to the human heart. God does not require the wounded to hide their fury; he invites them to bring it to him instead of acting on it. C. S. Lewis, in Reflections on the Psalms (1958), gave a chapter to these cursing psalms, arguing that they show both the evil that injustice breeds in its victims and the moral seriousness of people who refused to shrug at wrong.

Christians do not pray this verse as a model to imitate. They read it through the teaching of Jesus to love enemies and through Paul's instruction to leave vengeance to God. Some readers take the psalm's children as a figure for the future of an empire; others resist any softening and let the verse stand as the scream of the wounded. Either way, the psalm shows that raw anger can be carried into prayer, and that God, not the victim, is the one who will finally judge.

questions: The exiles could not sing the songs of Zion in Babylon. Have you ever found it impossible to worship the way you once did, and what did you do with that silence?
The psalm brings raw anger straight to God. What difference does it make to pray your anger rather than act on it or hide it?
How does the teaching of Jesus about enemies change the way a Christian reads and prays this psalm, without pretending its grief isn't real?
